name: Bargaining institutions (ICTWSS)
desc_html:
The institutional half of the OECD/AIAS ICTWSS database, version 2.0: whether the right to organise, to bargain and to strike is recognised, in the market sector and in government; at what level bargaining happens; whether agreements are extended by law to firms that never signed them; how wage setting is coordinated; whether works councils bargain over pay; whether a tripartite council exists.
OECD's statistical service publishes two variables from this database, union density and bargaining coverage. The rest is distributed only as a spreadsheet and appears in no SDMX service anywhere.
Most of these indicators are ordinal codes rather than quantities: a higher bargaining level means a different level, not more of something. The codebook defines each scale.
How to read these. Pick an indicator and the key for its scale appears under the chart, listing what each code means. Bargaining level, for instance, runs 1 for company bargaining through 3 for sector bargaining to 5 for central cross-industry bargaining. A line that steps from 3 to 1 is a country that moved wage setting from the industry to the firm, which is the single most consequential institutional change in European industrial relations since 1980. It is not a fall in a quantity.
Where a scale runs the other way, or where an indicator is a count rather than a code, the unit under the chart says so. The one continuous index here is centralization of bargaining, which combines level with the coverage and coordination behind it.
desc_text: The institutional half of the OECD/AIAS ICTWSS database: rights of association, collective bargaining and strike; bargaining level; mandatory extension; wage coordination; works councils; tripartite councils.

rAEB.3: additional enterprise bargaining on wages is common: more than half of employees covered by sector or central agreements are affected
rAEB.2: additional enterprise bargaining on wages occurs only in large firms: between 10 and 50 percent of employees covered by sector or central agreements are affected
rAEB.1: additional enterprise bargaining on wages is rare even in large firms: less than 10 percent of employees covered by sector or central agreements are affected
rAEB.0: no additional enterprise-level bargaining on wages; this including cases where such bargaining is explicitly forbidden Note: Where regional agreements are nested within sector agre

SPA_negot.1: Yes (to be registered in year in which pact or agreement is signed)
SPA_negot.-99: not applicable (no social pact or central agreement)
SPA_negot.2: Tripartite agreement, without one or more major union confederation(s)
SPA_negot.3: Tripartite agreement, without one or more major employers peak association(s)
SPA_negot.4: Tripartite (minority) agreement, without one or more major union confederation(s) and without one or more major employers’ peak association(s)
SPA_negot.5: Bipartite agreement, signed by all major (mainstream) union confederations and employers’ peak associations
SPA_negot.6: Bipartite agreement, without one or more major union confederation(s)
SPA_negot.7: Bipartite agreement, without one or more major employers’ peak association(s)
SPA_negot.8: Bipartite (minority) agreement, without one or more major union confederations and without one or more major employers’ peak federations
SPA_negot.9: Imposed or commuted by the government (Refers to the pact or agreement coded in SPA_Sign in case of more than one pact or agreement) 14 

TC.2: tripartite council with representation from the trade unions, employers’ associations, and independent experts or government (-appointed) representatives
TC.1: council with various societal interest representatives, including unions and employers

WC.2: existence and rights of works council or structure for (union and non-union based) employee representation within firms or establishments confronting management are mandated by law
WC.1: works councils (etc.) are voluntary, i.e. even where they are mandated by law, there are no legal sanctions for non-observance
WC.0: works council or similar (union or non-union) based institutions of employee representation confronting management do not exist or are exceptional

NMW.1: yes, but the statutory minimum wage(s) cover(s) only specific sectors, specific groups, occupations and/or regions
NMW.2: yes, at national level Coding rules: The variable is coded as 2 only when a statutory minimum wage exists at national/federal level. When statutory minimum wages exist only at subn

Ext.3: extension is virtually automatic and more or less general (including enlargement)
Ext.2: extension is used in many industries, but there are thresholds and Ministers can (and sometimes do) decide not to extend (clauses in) collective agreements
Ext.1: extension is rather exceptional, used in some industries only, because of absence of sector agreements, very high thresholds (supermajorities of 60% or more, public policy criteria
Ext.0: there are neither legal provisions for mandatory extension, nor is there a functional equivalent

MW_uprate.2: at the discretion of public institution or the body setting the minimum wage Coding rules: (1) a form of indexation (to price or other indicators) plays a formal role in the decisi

MW_comm.2: yes, somewhat binding Coding rules: (0) no such committee exists; (1) a consultative committee exists, but it plays only an advisory role and its advice does not need to be taken i

Level.5: wage bargaining predominantly takes place at the central or cross-industry level
Level.4: wage bargaining intermediates or alternates between the central and industry level
Level.3: wage bargaining predominantly takes place at the sector or industry level
Level.2: wage bargaining intermediates or alternates between the sector and enterprise level
Level.1: bargaining predominantly takes place at the company or enterprise level. 

Multilevel.7: cross-sectoral (entire economy or private sector), with centrally determined binding norms, minima or ceilings to be respected by all further agreements, which can only implement c
Multilevel.6: cross-sectoral (entire economy or private sector) and sectoral, with sectoral agreements that specify and can deviate from central agreements, guidelines or targets
Multilevel.5: cross-sectoral (entire economy or private sector), sectoral and company, with company agreements that specify and can deviate from sector agreements, and sector agreements that spe
Multilevel.4: cross-sectoral (entire economy or private sector) and company, with company agreements that specify and can deviate from central agreements
Multilevel.3: sectoral (separate branches of the economy), with sectorally determined binding norms, minima or ceilings to be respected by all further agreements and company or enterprise agreem
Multilevel.2: sectoral (separate branches of the economy) and company, with company agreements that specify and can deviate from sectorally agreed norms, guidelines or targets

Art.1: articulated: additional enterprise bargaining on wages is recognized and takes place under control of the ‘outside’ union, i.e. the signatory or signatories of sector and company a
Art.2: partially articulated: additional enterprise bargaining on wages takes place under control of the (non- union) works council; the signatory or signatories of sector and company agr
Art.3: disarticulated bargaining; additional enterprise bargaining on wages when it happens is, formally or informally, also conducted by non-union bodies and not answerable to or under c

DR.1: it is possible to derogate from terms established by law (and offer less favourable conditions) by means of collective agreement
DR.0: it is not possible to derogate from the law

FAV.3: favourability is inversed, terms in lower level agreements take precedence
FAV.2: hierarchy between levels is undefined and a matter for the negotiating parties (not fixed in law)
FAV.1: Lower-level agreements must by law offer more favourable terms, but exceptions possible under defined conditions
FAV.0: Hierarchy between agreement-levels is strictly applied and defined in law: lower-level agreements can only offer more favourable terms

WSSA.2: sectoral agreements set the framework or define the default for enterprise bargaining
WSSA.1: sectoral agreements define the minimum wage level (and minimum rate changes)
WSSA.0: sectoral agreements define the minimum and actual levels (and rate changes) of wages

OCG.2: sectoral agreements contain opening clauses, allowing the renegotiation of contractual wages at enterprise level
OCG.1: sectoral agreements contain opening clauses, allowing the renegotiation of contractual non-wage issues (working hours, working time schedules, unsocial hours, etc.) at enterprise l
OCG.0: sectoral agreements contain no opening clauses

OCT.1: agreements (at any level) contain crisis-related opening clauses, defined as temporary changes, renegotiation or suspension of contractual provisions, under defined hardship condit

Index.1: (most or many) collective agreements contain (semi-) automatic index or cost-of living escalator clauses, linking wages to prices
Index.0: use of index clauses is rare or forbidden

WC_type.2: works councils is composed of employees (employee-only council)
WC_type.1: works councils is composed of employees and employer (or employer representative), or chaired by (or on behalf of) employers (joint council)
WC_type.0: works council does not exist or is most exceptional

WC_struct.3: single-channel works councils, union-based representation, elected by union members or established by union, based on law or national agreement
WC_struct.2: dual-channel works councils, union dominated representation, elected by union and non-union members, based on law or national agreement
WC_struct.1: split-channel works councils, employee elected works councils are mandatory where there is no or insufficient union representation, as a structure supplementary to the union, based

UWRep.2: yes, this is mandatory or guaranteed under a basic general agreement between unions and employers
UWRep.1: yes, but only where unions are recognised and have negotiated an agreement

Coord.5: Binding norms regarding maximum or minimum wage rates or wage increases issued as a result of a) centralized bargaining by the central union and employers’ associations, with or wi
Coord.3: Procedural negotiation guidelines (recommendations on, for instance, wage demand formula relating to productivity or inflation) issued by a) the government or government agency, an
Coord.2: Some coordination of wage setting, based on pattern setting by major companies, sectors, government wage policies in the public sector, judicial awards, or minimum wage policies
Coord.1: Fragmented wage bargaining, confined largely to individual firms or plants, no coordination 12 
Coord.4: wage norms set by one-off central agreements, or by pattern bargaining with a dominant leader

Peace.2: strikes may not be called over the terms of the collective agreement while the agreement is in force (which implies a peace clause)
Peace.1: there is no (implicit or explicit) legal obligation, but in practice most (private sector) collective agreements contain a peace clause
Peace.0: no peace obligation or peace clause

WC_rights.3: economic and social rights, including codetermination on some issues (e.g., mergers, take-overs, restructuring, etc.)
WC_rights.2: economic and social rights, consultation (advice, with possibility of judicial redress)
WC_rights.1: information and consultation rights (without judicial redress)
WC_rights.0: works council or similar (union or non-union) based institutions of employee representation confronting management do not exist or are exceptional. 

Govint.5: the government imposes private sector wage settlements, places a ceiling on bargaining outcomes or suspends bargaining
Govint.4: the government participates directly in wage bargaining (tripartite bargaining, as in social pacts)
Govint.3: the government influences wage bargaining outcomes indirectly through price-ceilings, indexation, tax measures, minimum wages, and/or pattern setting through public sector wages
Govint.2: the government influences wage bargaining by providing an institutional framework of consultation and information exchange, by conditional agreement to extend private sector agreem
Govint.1: none of the above. Conflict resolution and enforcement of agreements

Type.6: Government-imposed bargaining (incl. statutory controls in lieu of bargaining)
Type.5: Government-sponsored bargaining (this includes social pacts, provided they deal with wages)
Type.1: Government sets signals (public sector wages, minimum wage)

WC_negot.4: works councils (or mandated representatives) formally negotiate (plant-level) collective agreements, alongside or instead of trade unions
WC_negot.3: works councils (or mandated representatives) formally negotiate (plant-level) collective agreements, if no union is present (and/or subject to ballot)
WC_negot.2: works councils is formally (by law or agreement) barred from negotiating (plant-level) agreements, but informally negotiate over workplace-related working conditions or ‘employment
WC_negot.1: works councils is formally (by law or agreement) barred from negotiating (plant-level) agreements and involvement of works councils in negotiating (plant-level) agreements is rare
